svg.title: An everyday change goes from an issue to a released version — An issue becomes a merge request, and main releases the change
svg.text: An everyday change goes from an issue to a released
Scenario: An issue becomes a merge request, and main releases the change
The change rides a merge request

g.text: Given an installed project with the framework already on its main
branch
A project that already ran the installer: main carries the whole framework, with its
automation token wired so the release can run on its own. This is where a new day of work
begins.
When the developer opens an issue for a small change
An issue is a ticket describing the work. This one asks for a short line in the README.
Opening it first is how a change starts here.
Then a merge request opens from the issue, with its own branch
A merge request (the page where a change is reviewed before joining main) is created
straight from the issue, together with the branch that will carry the work.
When the developer checks out the branch and edits the README
The developer switches to the new branch and adds one line to the README. This is the
everyday change the whole story is about.
And the developer commits the change as a conventional feat
The commit message follows Conventional Commits (feat: a new feature), so the release
tooling can turn it into the next version later.

text.tspan: git commit -m "feat: mention the toolbox in the readme"

g.text: And the developer pushes the branch to GitLab
Pushing the branch updates the merge request and starts its pipeline (the automatic checks
that must pass before the change can merge).
Then the merge request's pipeline turns green
The full inherited pipeline runs on the change and every job passes. Main only accepts a
change once these checks are green.
When the reviewed change merges into main
With the pipeline green, the merge request is merged. The branch joins main through review,
never a forced push.
Then main's pipeline stamps the next version tag
The merge starts main's own pipeline; its release job reads the feat commit and stamps the
next version. The tags page now shows 0.2.0 — plain, with no v in front.
And the new version now lives in the files on main
The release wrote the change into the repository: the README now carries the developer's
line and VERSION reads 0.2.0. The everyday contribution is proven end to end.
